The study aims to develop an automated system for the detection and classification of abnormal red blood cells using computer vision techniques.
The proposed system utilizes image processing algorithms to extract relevant features from microscopic images of blood samples.
These features are then used to train a machine learning model for the classification of normal and abnormal red blood cells.
The performance of the system is evaluated using a dataset of blood samples with known abnormalities.
The results show that the proposed system achieves high accuracy in the classification of abnormal red blood cells, demonstrating its potential for use in clinical settings for the early detection of blood disorders.

At higher concentrations, the system transitions to an equilibrium gel phase, where the particles form a network-like structure.
The authors also investigate the effect of particle size and concentration on the formation of these phases.
Overall, this study provides insights into the behavior of colloidal clay systems and contributes to our understanding of the self-assembly of colloidal particles.

To address these issues, we propose a fully octave CNN architecture that leverages octave convolutional layers to capture multi-scale information efficiently.
Our network achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets while being significantly faster and more memory-efficient than existing methods.
Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed approach for document image segmentation.

Interactive image segmentation is a challenging task in computer vision that requires accurately segmenting objects of interest from an image with user interaction.
In this paper, we propose a fully convolutional two-stream fusion network for interactive image segmentation.
The network consists of two streams: a segmentation stream and an interaction stream.
The segmentation stream is responsible for generating initial segmentation masks, while the interaction stream is used to refine the segmentation masks based on user input.
We introduce a novel fusion module that combines the outputs of the two streams to produce the final segmentation result.
Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed network achieves state-of-the-art performance in interactive image segmentation.

We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and compare it to state-of-the-art methods.
The experimental results demonstrate that our CGRN model achieves competitive performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

In this paper, we challenge this assumption and propose a new perspective on data augmentation.

Our findings suggest that researchers and practitioners should reconsider the role of unseen domain generalization in data augmentation and explore alternative approaches that focus on improving model robustness and generalization rather than matching the test data distribution.

Our findings suggest that LeViT-UNet has the potential to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of medical image segmentation in clinical practice.

Land cover segmentation is a crucial task in remote sensing applications, as it provides valuable information for various environmental and urban planning studies.
However, the performance of land cover segmentation algorithms can be affected by differences in satellite sensors and acquisition conditions.
In this paper, we propose a domain adaptation approach to improve land cover segmentation across different satellites.
We first train a segmentation model on a source dataset from one satellite and then adapt it to a target dataset from a different satellite using domain adaptation techniques.
Specifically, we employ a domain adversarial neural network to align the feature distributions between the source and target domains.
Experimental results on two publicly available land cover datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach in improving land cover segmentation accuracy across different satellites.

TapLab utilizes a tap-based approach to efficiently process video frames by tapping into compressed-domain information.
We introduce a TapNet architecture that combines a tap-based encoder-decoder network with a compressed-domain feature extractor.
Our experiments demonstrate that TapLab achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both accuracy and speed on various benchmark datasets.
Furthermore, we show that TapLab is robust to compression artifacts and can effectively handle videos with different compression levels.

IPatch is a novel approach to generating adversarial patches that can be remotely applied to images to deceive deep learning models.
Unlike previous methods that require physical access to the target image, IPatch leverages the power of generative adversarial networks (GANs) to create patches that can be applied remotely.
The proposed method consists of two stages: patch generation and patch application.
In the patch generation stage, a GAN is trained to generate patches that are visually similar to the target image but contain adversarial perturbations.
In the patch application stage, the generated patch is applied to the target image remotely, fooling the deep learning model into misclassifying the image.
Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of IPatch in evading state-of-the-art deep learning models, highlighting the potential security risks associated with remote adversarial attacks.

However, obtaining a large-scale dataset with fully annotated labels for training deep learning models is often challenging due to the limited availability of expert annotations.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach for robust medical image segmentation on small-scale data with incomplete labels.
Our method leverages the concept of self-training and semi-supervised learning to effectively utilize the available labeled and unlabeled data.
We introduce a consistency regularization term to encourage the model to produce consistent predictions on unlabeled data, which helps improve the segmentation performance.
Additionally, we propose a novel uncertainty estimation technique to identify the most uncertain predictions and prioritize them for expert annotation, thereby iteratively improving the quality of the labeled data.

We evaluate SGCL on several benchmark datasets and compare it with state-of-the-art few-shot segmentation methods.
The experimental results demonstrate that SGCL achieves superior performance in terms of segmentation accuracy and generalization ability.

However, in many real-world scenarios, obtaining labeled source domain data is expensive or impractical.
To address this limitation, we introduce a source-free domain adaptation framework that leverages unlabeled source and target domain data.
Our approach combines a self-training strategy with a consistency regularization loss to encourage the model to produce consistent predictions on both domains.

This paper presents ACNN, a full resolution deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) for medical image segmentation.
ACNN is designed to address the challenges of segmenting medical images with high resolution and complex structures.
The network architecture consists of multiple convolutional layers followed by upsampling layers to preserve the full resolution of the input image.
ACNN also incorporates skip connections to enable information flow between different levels of the network.
The proposed network is trained using a combination of pixel-wise cross-entropy loss and Dice loss.
Experimental results on various medical image datasets demonstrate that ACNN achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency.
